findings.title: Crisis, rescue, and changed footing
findings.claim: When harm reaches the travelers at sea, the supports they call upon become unavailable; rescue separates them from that danger and brings them to land, after which they turn away and the human is called ungrateful. The preceding merciful sea passage and the following land and sea warnings make that withdrawal part of a sequence in which relief changes the footing without ending dependence.
findings.mechanism: The contact form meets the harm noun; the disappearance verb takes the objects supplied by the call, while the exception leaves one divine addressee; the rescue form then names separation with land as its endpoint. The 17:66 vessel-and-mercy setting leads into this scene, and 17:68-69 immediately question land's security and reopen sea danger. The focus turn and the favor-covering sense of the final predicate connect changed footing to the response.
findings.reader_payoff: The passage links the loss of invoked support, an extraction from danger, and a withdrawal after relief into one cause-and-response movement.
findings.containment: The ordinary sequence remains harm at sea, the sole exception, rescue to land, turning away, and ingratitude. The called-for beings are not claimed to vanish physically, and the channel's amnesia image is not a claim of literal memory loss or an explicit belief that land is self-securing.

epistemic.reason: The citable channel supports are trusted and the activated focus branches have supplied registry entries. The cross-ayah extension is bounded to the exact 17:66, 17:68, and 17:69 connections.

findings.containment: The packet supplies inducement, denied authority, and the focus turn; the causal arrow that the campaign conditions this turn is an inference. A simpler account of renewed ordinary human disposition remains live.

findings.claim: The focus rescue carries the travelers from sea to land within a pericope that presents directed passage, mercy, a keeper, renewed land danger, and the possibility of returning to sea. The destination changes, while the sequence keeps both media within continuing governance.
findings.mechanism: In 17:66 a keeper directs the vessel through the sea in mercy; 17:67 names rescue to land; 17:68 questions confidence as land can sink; 17:69 raises a return to sea and drowning. These distinct carriers and triggers make the focus endpoint a transition under continuing care rather than an independently securing medium.
findings.reader_payoff: Arrival on land remains a real rescue while the reader can see that changed geography does not itself end dependence.
findings.containment: The sequence supports continued governance and questions land's autonomy, but does not state that the travelers consciously believed land secured them. A narrower reading of 17:68-69 as warnings that danger can occur in either medium remains live.

epistemic.reason: The source trace is exact and macro-local, but its reconstructed HFT identity is legacy_unbound and its inference about assumed autonomy remains qualified.

In 17:71 the supplied call-role reverses, and leaders and written records give that later call a durable form; 17:72 adds blindness and straying on a path. Those specific contacts make emergency speech part of an inferred call-and-accountability arc.

findings.containment: This is a pericope-level relation, not a claim that both calls are the same utterance or that the focus explicitly predicts the later scene. The packet's alternative of thematic juxtaposition without a deliberate arc remains live.

findings.title: Orientation under continuing pressure
findings.claim: The focus turn is set beside a later sequence in which pressure tries to incline the prophet, stabilization prevents that near-turn, expulsion from the land is threatened, and an unchanging course closes the scene. Read together, these contacts make orientation vulnerable to renewed pressure rather than permanently settled by crisis recognition.
findings.mechanism: The focus side-turn is the carrier; the later pressure, near-inclination, stabilization, threatened departure from land, and fixed course are independent contextual triggers. Their contrast with the completed turn changes the focus into one episode within a pericope where orientation is tested and sustained.
findings.reader_payoff: The land arrival does not guarantee durable recognition; the pericope keeps attention on how orientation is maintained under later pressure.
findings.containment: The focus addresses plural travelers, while 17:73-77 addresses the prophet and describes a near-inclination prevented by stabilization. The relation is a contextual comparison, not a same-person or direct-causation claim; the possibility that the later sequence is separate remains live.

findings.title: The invoked network as pressure
findings.claim: The focus calling form can also carry the packet's split-root image of forceful pushing: the invoked network presses on conduct in ease, while the same crisis sequence shows those supports unavailable when real rescue is needed.
findings.mechanism: The qualified push branch on the focus call meets the preceding pericope's destabilizing solicitation, and the focus disappearance branch supplies the counter-contact of supports failing in crisis. This changes the call from a purely passive request into an exploratory picture of dependencies that can shape conduct yet fail as effective aid.
findings.reader_payoff: The called-for network can be perceived as exerting pressure on conduct as well as standing as a hoped-for source of help.
findings.containment: The ordinary surface remains calling or invocation. The physical-pushing branch is not asserted as the lexical translation, 17:64 is not identified as every invoked support, and the pressure-system relation remains exploratory.

epistemic.reason: The outlier is an exact but legacy-unbound HFT trace; its source explicitly marks the split-root contact as exploratory and bounds it away from the lexical meaning.

findings.title: Exclusive worship and aid
findings.claim: The focus's call culminates in one remaining addressee; the added 1:5 names worship and asking for aid as practices directed to You alone. The turn after rescue can therefore be heard against an explicit practice of dependence that extends beyond the emergency.
findings.mechanism: The focus call and exception provide the carrier and focus return; the external worship and aid-seeking forms supply a distinct trigger. Their contact adds the semantic detail of worship and assistance-seeking to the focus's emergency appeal and makes the post-rescue turn a break in that relation.
findings.reader_payoff: The sole addressee in danger is connected with an explicit pattern of worship and aid-seeking that does not end when the travelers reach land.
findings.containment: This overlay uses only the supplied 1:5 wording and does not claim that 17:67 quotes it or that the whole Fatiha is a frame. The focus's rescue and turning remain complete in their own terms.

epistemic.reason: The focus and external text, including their exact word positions, are supplied; the link between the two is a bounded contextual inference rather than an attributed source claim.

branch_activations.boundary: The contact is a local overlay; it is not evidence that the focus quotes 1:5.
